### Output:

```
PMID 25451447
TITLE Soft drink consumption is associated with depressive symptoms among adults in China.
ABSTRACT Research evidence supports a positive link between soft drinks and depressive symptoms. However, data thus far are only from Caucasian populations. We investigated whether high levels of consumption of soft drinks were associated with the depressive symptoms among adults in China. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 3667 adults in Tianjin, China. Dietary intake was assessed using a valid self-administered food frequency questionnaire, and depressive symptoms were assessed with the Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS), cut-off point of 40, 45 or 50 indicating elevated depressive symptoms. The prevalence of elevated depressive symptoms was 7.6% (SDS ≥50). After adjustments for potentially confounding factors, the odds ratios (95% confidence interval) of having elevated depressive symptoms by increasing levels of soft drink consumption were 1.00, 1.43 (1.01, 2.01) and 2.00 (1.15, 3.37) (p for trend <0.01). Similar relations were observed when SDS ≥40 or 45 were used as a definition of depressive symptoms. This is a cross-sectional study, causal relation remains unknown. Our results suggested that high consumption of soft drinks was significantly related to a higher prevalence of depressive symptoms among adults in China. This is the first large cross-sectional study addressing this topic in an Asia population.

PMID 31097051
TITLE Daily intake of soft drinks is associated with symptoms of anxiety and depression in Chinese adolescents.
ABSTRACT The association of soft drink consumption with mental problems in Asian adolescents has not been reported. The present study aimed to investigate the association of soft drink consumption and symptoms of anxiety and depression in adolescents in China. A cross-sectional study to investigate the association of intake of soft drinks and sugars from soft drinks with symptoms of anxiety and depression measured by the two-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-2) and the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-2), respectively. A comprehensive university in Changsha, China. Newly enrolled college students in 2017. In total, 8226 students completed the investigation and 8085 students with no systemic disorders were finally analysed. Students consuming soft drinks ≥7 times/week had significantly higher (mean difference; 95 % CI) GAD-2 (0·15; 0·07, 0·23) and PHQ-2 (0·27; 0·19, 0·35) scores compared with those barely consuming soft drinks, adjusted for demographic and behavioural factors. Those consuming >25 g sugar/d from soft drinks had significantly higher GAD-2 (0·11; 0·04, 0·18) and PHQ-2 (0·22; 0·15, 0·29) scores compared with non-consumers. The mediation effect of obesity in the associations was not clinically significant. Adolescents consuming soft drinks ≥7 times/week, or >25 g sugar/d from soft drinks, had significantly higher levels of anxiety and depression. Dietary suggestion is needed to prevent anxiety and depression in adolescents.

PMID 40529599
TITLE Sugar-sweetened beverage consumption and depressive symptoms among college students in northeastern China: The mediating role of mobile phone use addiction.
ABSTRACT Previous studies have explored the link between sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) consumption and depressive symptoms, but the mediating role of Mobile Phone Use Addiction (MPUA) remains unclear. This study aims to examine how MPUA mediates the relationship between SSB consumption and depressive symptoms among college students in Northeast China. A prospective study was conducted with first-year university freshmen across three northeastern Chinese provinces. MPUA was assessed using the Adolescent Problematic Mobile Phone Use Self-Rating Questionnaire, and depressive symptoms were measured with the 9-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9). Generalized linear regression models were used to analyze the relationships, and structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to test MPUA's mediating effect. MPUA and depressive symptoms were present in 27.3 % and 36.2 % of participants, respectively. After adjusting for confounders, significant associations were found between SSB consumption (e.g., fruit drinks, tea beverages) and depressive symptoms in both genders. SEM revealed that MPUA accounted for 47.0 % of the total indirect effect in the relationship between SSB consumption and depressive symptoms. This study highlights the mediating role of MPUA in the SSB-depression relationship among college students in Northeast China. These findings suggest the need for interventions targeting both mobile phone addiction and dietary habits to improve mental health. Future research should explore the mechanisms and generalizability of these results.

```

The strongest directly applicable result is the Tianjin adult cross-sectional study (n=3,667): adjusted odds increased across soft-drink intake levels, reaching OR 2.00 (95% CI 1.15–3.37) for the highest category versus the reference, with a significant trend. It supports an association but cannot establish causality. The newer Northeast-China college study offers convergent support, but college-age participants are not representative of all adults and the abstract provides no specific effect estimate. **Yes—soft-drink consumption was associated with depressive symptoms in a study of adults in China.** A cross-sectional survey of 3,667 adults in Tianjin found that, compared with the lowest intake category, the adjusted odds of elevated depressive symptoms (Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale score ≥50) were higher in the middle category (OR 1.43, 95% CI 1.01–2.01) and highest category (OR 2.00, 95% CI 1.15–3.37), with a significant trend (p<0.01). Similar patterns were reported using other symptom cutoffs (PMID: 25451447).

This supports an **association**, not a causal conclusion: the study was cross-sectional, so it cannot determine whether soft-drink intake preceded depressive symptoms or rule out residual confounding. A separate Chinese college-student study also reported higher depression symptom scores with frequent soft-drink intake, but it is less representative of adults overall (PMID: 31097051).

FINAL DECISION: YES
